rows.reference: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.4.1 (Book I, Lecture 4 'Righteousness', Lesson 1; Jacobi, SBE 22, p. 36)
rows.original: savve pāṇā savve bhūyā savve jīvā savve sattā na hantavvā (as recorded in households annex row JA-2; not displayed in any search output seen)
rows.says: The Arhats and Bhagavats of past, present and future all declare that no breathing, existing, living or sentient creature may be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented or driven away. The text calls this the pure, unchangeable, eternal law. Jacobi's footnote reads the fourfold phrase as 'all sorts of living beings'.
rows.bearing: K1: taught for the Śvetāmbara branch by a wider rule (rule 7). It reaches every person from birth, of any faith, status, sex or age, and states no exception, not even defence; K1 permits defence but does not require it, so a stricter rule still teaches K1. Book I is a monastic manual, but the sentence is given as the declaration of all Arhats, not as a monks' rule. K0: taught (narrower than K1). K3: the same wider rule reaches non-combatants. Does not speak for Digambaras (branch rule). The deciding Śvetāmbara text for all three wordings.

rows.reference: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.4.2 (Book I, Lecture 4, Lesson 2; Jacobi, SBE 22)
rows.says: Some brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas teach that all sorts of living beings may be slain, abused, tormented or driven away and that there is no wrong in it. The text calls this the doctrine of the unworthy, and gives the teachers' doctrine that no living being should be slain, tormented or driven off. It asks such teachers whether pain is pleasant to them: as it is unpleasant to them, so it is to all beings.
rows.bearing: Rejects in so many words any teaching that some killing is free of wrong, which bears against the kind of 'wholly blameless' killing that rule 2 describes. The opposing view is reported only to be rejected, so it is not counter-evidence (rule 4). K1 and K0: taught for Śvetāmbaras by a wider rule (rule 7).

rows.reference: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 ('On Activity'; Jacobi, SBE 45), the thirteen kinds of activity (kriyāsthāna), kinds 1 to 3; the first kind is in Jacobi's section 5; other paragraph numbers not displayed
rows.says: The first kind of sinful activity is injuring movable or immovable beings for one's own sake, or for relatives, household or spirits. The second is sin without personal interest. The third, called 'slaying', is killing movable or immovable beings because one thinks someone has hurt, hurts or will hurt oneself or one's own, whether one kills, has others kill or consents to it. In each case bad karma accrues to the doer.
rows.bearing: K0: Explicit for Śvetāmbaras as a wider rule: the canon faults injury done for one's own gain (kind 1) and killing done in revenge or to forestall a feared harm (kind 3). Kind 3 also counts killing someone who 'hurts' one now as sinful activity, which is stricter than K1's exception (K1 permits defence but does not require it), so it still teaches K1 (rule 7) and is not counter-evidence.

rows.says: A vow is turning away from injury (hiṃsā), falsehood, theft, unchastity and possessiveness. Kept in part it is the lesser vow (aṇuvrata, for householders); kept in full it is the great vow (mahāvrata, for ascetics).
rows.bearing: Shared counted text for every branch. Abstaining from injury to any living being is the first vow, and 7.2 makes it binding on householders in a lesser form. The sūtra does not itself say which part householders keep; the tradition's lay manuals (row on Ratnakaraṇḍaka 3.53, Tier 2) put intentional injury of any moving being, every human included, inside the forbidden minimum. A wider rule (rule 7) for K1 and K0 for all branches, the Digambara branch included. One of the deciding texts for Digambaras.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule); the householder's share is not specified in the sūtra itself

rows.reference: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.8 (Śvetāmbara) = 7.13 (Digambara), read with 7.1
rows.translation: herenow4u.net English (Śvetāmbara numbering 07.08; attributed in a search summary to Manu Doshi): 'Deprival of life on account of non-vigilance constitutes violence'. For the Digambara text (7.13): 'Injury is the severance of vitalities out of passion' (jainqq.org 006936/54; Wikipedia's 'Ahimsa in Jainism' gives the same wording from Vijay K. Jain's edition with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi), and V. A. Sangave, Jaina Path of Ahimsa, citing 7/13. Also a jainqq.org study book (JES 401)
rows.says: Injury (hiṃsā) is depriving a being of life through non-vigilant activity (pramatta-yoga). The Śvetāmbara-numbered edition's commentary says non-vigilance covers negligence and wrong motive: a surgeon whose patient dies in a needed operation does not commit violence, a careless one does. A study book glosses the phrase as an act involving negligence, attachment or aversion. On the Digambara side the sūtra is rendered 'the severance of vitalities out of passion', a person actuated by passion being called pramatta, and Sangave (citing 7/13) explains pramattayoga as activity driven by the passions that agitate mind, body or speech.
rows.bearing: Defines what the first vow forbids. Deliberate killing for gain or out of anger, hatred or revenge is a central case of an act driven by passion (anger and greed are among the passions), so with 7.1 the shared text teaches K0 and, as a wider rule, K1 for every branch (rule 7). Killing without negligence or passion falls outside the definition (exclusion (f)). The passion reading is now seen on both sides: in the Śvetāmbara-numbered edition's commentary and in Digambara-numbered renderings. It comes from translation and commentary, not from the sūtra's bare words. One of the deciding texts for Digambaras.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule); for K0's motives Clear teaching close to Explicit

rows.reference: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.20 (Śvetāmbara) = 7.25 (Digambara): the five lapses (aticāra) of the householder's vow of non-injury
rows.translation: Vijay K. Jain (2018, Digambara recension, with the Sarvārthasiddhi); Manu Doshi (2007, Śvetāmbara recension), who renders vadha 'fatal hurting'
rows.says: Binding, beating, mutilating, overloading and withholding food and drink from living beings are lapses of the householder's vow of non-injury.
rows.bearing: Shows that the lay vow reaches beings in one's power and that even lesser harms are faults against it, for every branch; deliberate killing, the core breach, is covered by 7.1 with 7.8 = 7.13. Supporting for K1 and K0 (rule 7). On the minority rendering of vadha as 'fatal hurting', killing a being in one's power would be listed as a lapse, which is still a fault; on either reading the text does not permit it. The meaning of vadha is open (Register Q-002) but does not change K1.

rows.says: Cultivate friendship towards all living beings, gladness (admiration) towards the virtuous, compassion towards the afflicted, and equanimity towards the ill-behaved or unteachable (avineya, 'the inveterate').
rows.bearing: Bears on 'the wicked': the one text every branch accepts prescribes equanimity, not hostility, towards the ill-behaved, and friendliness towards all beings. It does not speak of killing, so it is Implied for K1, but it shows that no class of persons is placed outside the duty of goodwill. No counted text was found that makes the wicked, unbelievers or heretics open to private killing.

rows.original: kṛta, kārita, mananāt ... sthūla-vadha-viramaṇa (pieces shown in the results; full verse not displayed)
rows.translation: English renderings on JainWorld (translators not identified; two renderings differ on whether approval is included). Champat Rai Jain (1917, public domain) not checked.
rows.says: Never intentionally injuring moving beings (those with two or more senses) by mind, speech or body, whether by doing it, having it done or approving it, is what the wise call the householder's vow against gross injury (ahiṃsā aṇuvrata). One rendering omits approval. A later writer, Amitagati, is reported to limit householders to six of the nine ways.
rows.bearing: Defines the householder's minimum under Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.2: every human is a moving being, so intentional killing of any person is forbidden to every lay Digambara. Clarifies the shared Tier 1 text; does not decide on its own (rule 1). The approval question does not affect K1, which concerns killing oneself. Note that this Digambara statement, as rendered, carries no 'innocent' qualifier.

rows.reference: Upāsakadaśā (Uvāsagadasāo) 1: the householder Ānanda's first lay vow (paragraph number not seen)
rows.translation: A. F. R. Hoernle (1888 to 1890), not seen; an unidentified English rendering reproduced on jainqq.org

On the standard reading 'gross' means injury to moving beings, which includes every person, but that definition and any 'innocent' or 'compulsion' qualifier were not shown (see the modern gloss row). Supports K1 and K0 for Śvetāmbara lay people (rule 7); the deciding Śvetāmbara text remains Ācārāṅga I.4.1.

rows.reference: Modern gloss of the first lay vow (sthūla-prāṇātipāta-viramaṇa) in a published book scanned on jainqq.org (011048, p. 29; title and author not shown in the search)
rows.says: The first lay vow is described as giving up the intentional, purposeless destruction of harmless beings that move freely. The lay share of non-injury is put (as the summary phrased it) at about one-twentieth and a quarter of the full vow, because plants, water and other stationary beings are left out.
rows.bearing: Confirms, as modern exposition only, the four limits of the lay vow that the Yogaśāstra row records from memory: moving beings only, intentional injury only, harmless (innocent) beings only, and injury without need. 'Harmless' leaves injury to an offender outside what the lay vow promises. If 'offender' means an attacker, that is K1's exception; if it reached a non-attacking wrongdoer killed privately, the lay vow would not forbid it, though the tradition would still count it as injury (Ācārāṅga I.4.1; Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2, third kind). Outside the corpus, so it never decides (rule 1); its classical source, if any, is the main open risk for the Śvetāmbara lay case.

rows.reference: Fourfold division of a householder's injury: intentional (saṅkalpī), domestic (ārambhī), occupational (udyogī) and defensive (virodhī), as set out in V. A. Sangave, Jaina Path of Ahimsa (pp. 33 and 68), and on JainWorld
rows.says: The householder must give up intentional injury; domestic, occupational and defensive injury cannot be fully avoided at the householder's stage, so they do not break the lay vow, though they remain injury to be kept to a minimum. Defensive injury is described as committed 'in the defence of person and property against assailants and enemies', and elsewhere as killing a violent attacker in defence of oneself or others. Some summaries extend it to thieves, robbers, dacoits or enemies in battle, and to defending one's country; aggression is 'strongly discouraged'. A twofold division (occupational and intentional) also appears.
rows.bearing: Matches K1's exception for defending oneself or others. The mention of property and of thieves goes beyond K1's exception (killing only to stop killing or grave harm); no counted text was found that allows killing to defend property alone. Modern and untraced, so it never decides (rule 1). If a classical commentary were found to allow lethal force for property alone, the reach of the lay vow could become Unclear (rule 6).

rows.says: Lead only: the householder's partial vow gives up intentional injury of mobile beings, and one-sensed stationary beings are not covered. From memory, the verse states the vow for 'innocent' (nirāgas) mobile beings, and Śvetāmbara lay teaching explains the householder's share by four limits: only mobile beings, only intentional injury, only the innocent (niraparādha), and only injury done without need (nirapekṣa). The four limits are now seen in a modern gloss (separate row); the classical verse is not.
rows.bearing: If confirmed, a classical Śvetāmbara narrowing of the lay vow that leaves injury to an 'offender' outside it. Whether 'offender' means an attacker (inside K1's exception), a criminal punished by the ruler (context, rule 5), or anyone who has done wrong and is killed privately and not in defence (against K1) is exactly what the commentary would settle. Tier 2 and Śvetāmbara only, so it cannot decide on its own (rule 1); but because rule 6 lets a classical commentator's narrowing of a counted text make a label Unclear, this is the main unverified risk to the Śvetāmbara lay case. Even then the Śvetāmbara wider rule (Ācārāṅga I.4.1) and Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 (which faults killing in revenge or pre-emptively) would stand. The stationary-beings point concerns plants and the elements (exclusion (e) by analogy).

rows.topic: support and limit; context: ruler's order
rows.reference: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 ('Nālandā'; Jacobi, SBE 45, Udaka from p. 420; jainqq.org scan of Jacobi pp. 470 to 474), Udaka Peḍhālaputta's objection to the lay vow and Gautama's reply; paragraph not confirmed
rows.says: Udaka, son of Peḍhāla, a follower of Pārśva, reports that Nirgrantha monks have a householder renounce injury to movable beings, 'except on the order of an established authority' (wording as shown in a search summary of Jacobi), with the example of a householder who has one of the captured thieves set free. Jacobi's note links the example to a commentator's apologue of a king who spared one of six sons, the six standing for the six classes of living beings, and explains that a householder, unable to give up injuring all beings as monks do, limits his vow to movable beings. The debate that follows turns on whether such a vow can be kept, since beings pass between movable and immovable births; it includes the remark that some, from anger or greed, make householders take the renunciation in a faulty form (who says this was not clearly shown). Gautama defends the vow as valid when rightly understood.
rows.bearing: Supporting, and a limit. The lay vow it describes covers all movable beings, which includes every human, so this Tier 1 text puts every person from birth inside the Śvetāmbara lay vow (a wider rule for K1 and K0). Its one exception is the order of an established authority, which is a ruler's order: context for K1 and K0 (rule 5, exclusions (a) and (b)). An exception to a vow says what the vow does not cover; the text, as far as seen, does not say the excepted killing is right, so it presupposes rather than approves and does not contradict K1 (rule 4). For K3 it is the nearest counted text on a lay person under orders, and the same reading is applied (see the K3 label). Open: whether the exception reaches orders from non-rulers. In Bhagavatī 7.9 Varuṇa is compelled to fight by 'the king, the assembly and the army', which fits reading the exception, in war, as public authority.
rows.strength: Clear teaching that the lay vow covers every human (supporting); n/a as a limit (context)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), partly: continuation searches 24 and 25 returned sacred-texts.com sbe4571 (Book 2, Lecture 7) with a summary giving the vow to renounce injury to movable beings 'except on the order of an established authority', the thief example and Jacobi's note on the king and the six sons, and a jainqq.org scan of Jacobi (011060/470) with Gautama's reply. Earlier: counter search 1 (sbe4571, the same formula and example) and counter search 4 (jainqq.org 011060/470 to 472: the Nālandā lecture's opening and the follower who has renounced injury to movable but not immovable beings). Jacobi's index places Udaka at pp. 420 ff. The Prakrit word (abhioga, from memory), the paragraph number and the exact sentences were not shown. Not read directly.
rows.check: searched and confirmed in part. Corrected: the exception now reads, as shown, 'on the order of an established authority' (not 'compulsion'); the scope of the lay vow (movable beings, so every human), Jacobi's note on the six sons and Gautama's defence of the vow added; bearing now records the row as supporting as well as limiting. Speakers of individual remarks still not clearly shown.

rows.reference: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 (Nālandā; Jacobi, SBE 45, from p. 420; jainqq.org scan of Jacobi p. 470), Gautama's reply to Udaka: the analogy of the 'renegade' householder; paragraph not confirmed
rows.says: In his reply Gautama asks whether a man breaks his word if he puts to death a 'renegade' householder, and the answer given is no. He then applies the same reasoning to a lay follower who has renounced injury to movable beings but not to immovable ones: if he kills immovable beings he does not break his vow. As remembered (not seen), the man's vow covered only those who had entered the order, and the victim had left it.
rows.bearing: A debating analogy about how far a vow reaches: a narrow vow is not broken by killing someone outside its terms. It does not say the killing is right or free of fault. In the same reply the follower's killing of immovable beings is said not to break his vow, yet the Jain texts count all such killing as injury that brings bad karma (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2; Ācārāṅga I.4.1). So 'does not break his vow' is not 'blameless' (rule 2 not met). The passage presupposes a narrow vow and does not approve the killing: Implied, does not decide (rule 4). Recorded as the nearest Tier 1 Jain text to a 'killing without breach' case, so that the hard case is visible. A reviewer should read the passage in full, because the search did not show who made the vow or its exact terms.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search), in outline only: continuation search 25 returned a jainqq.org scan of Jacobi, SBE 45 (011060/470), with Gautama asking whether a man breaks his word by putting to death a 'renegade' householder (answer: no) and the application to immovable beings; continuation search 24's summary described the same analogy but garbled who kills whom. rows.reference: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti, Viyāhapannatti) 7.9 (cited in scholarship as BhS 7.9.301): Varuṇa in the Rathamusala battle
rows.translation: J. Deleu, Viyāhapannatti (1970), and an English Bhagavatī translation, both as shown on jainqq.org; Āgam edition with Hindi on jainqq.org
rows.says: Varuṇa, grandson of Nāga, a lay follower of Mahāvīra in Vaiśālī serving under King Ceṭaka, is compelled by the king, the assembly and the army to join the Rathamusala battle. He vows to fight only a man who strikes him first. Wounded by such a man, he kills him, leaves the field, takes the monastic vows, dies, and is reborn in the Sohamma (Saudharma) heaven; a friend is reborn in a good human family; gods shower fragrant rain in his honour. The passage takes up the popular belief that the many killed in such battles are reborn among the gods and corrects it: most combatants are reborn in hell or as animals.
rows.bearing: War is context for K1 and K0 (rule 5, exclusion (b)). The text approves, through his rebirth, a lay follower who under orders strikes only at an attacker, which fits K1's exception, and it rejects the belief that death in battle earns heaven. For K3 the vow would spare everyone not fighting, but it is one man's vow, not a stated rule: Implied (rule 4).

rows.reference: Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya, verses 79 to 89
rows.translation: Vijay K. Jain (2012), as summarised on Wikipedia
rows.says: Eleven verses warn householders against excuses put forward for killing: that gods or religion are served by it, that suffering beings should be killed out of mercy, that beings who are happy or in meditation should be killed so that their state carries into the next life, and that killing oneself or others frees the soul. From memory, the same verses also reject killing harmful creatures to protect many, or sinners to stop them adding to their wrongs, and killing one's teacher at his request; not confirmed.
rows.bearing: The Digambara tradition's own answer to proposed exceptions: motive (religion, mercy, the victim's state) does not make killing right. Supports K1 and K0 for Digambaras at Tier 2 (not counted on its own, rule 1) and bears against declaring any killing blameless because of the victim's state or act.

rows.tier: 2 (Śvetāmbara exegetical layer: accepted by Mūrtipūjakas; not binding for Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs)
rows.reference: Niśītha Cūrṇi (on Niśītha Bhāṣya gāthā 289, as cited by a secondary book) and, as reported, Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya: rules for emergencies, defence of the community (saṅgha) and of a nun under assault; primary passages not seen
rows.says: Modern Jain writers report that the Niśītha Cūrṇi (verse 289, as cited) lets monks, not only householders, use force to protect the religious order or a virtuous woman's modesty, and that it is the monks' duty to act forcefully 'for the defence and justice of' a young nun who is assaulted. One such book argues that these acts, though they look violent, count as non-violent when done without selfish motive or hatred, and gives Ācārya Kālaka and King Ceṭaka as examples of such 'exceptional' non-violence. Another secondary source adds that monastic followers 'resorted to the common dictum for the laymen that an enemy of Dharma must be punished', and notes critics who saw this as ends justifying means.
rows.bearing: Defending a person or the community under attack is within K1's exception, so the core cases, as described, do not contradict K1. The reported dictum that an enemy of the faith must be punished is the nearest thing found to a zealot rule in Jain literature: if a primary passage let a monk or lay person kill an 'enemy of the faith' who is not then attacking, on his own authority, it would bear against K1 for the Mūrtipūjaka sub-branch. But it is Tier 2 (not treated as primary: the tradition places the cūrṇis below the Āgamas), untraced, and known only from loosely worded modern summaries, so it cannot decide (rule 1). Recorded so the hard case is visible.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search) only as secondary reports: the first session's search 19 returned a jainqq.org book on positive non-violence (006917/38) citing Niśītha Cūrṇi verse 289 on force to protect the order or a woman's modesty, with the 'no selfish motive or hatred' reading, and confirmed Granoff's article as 'The Violence of Non-Violence: A Study of Some Jain Responses to Non-Jain Religious Practices', JIABS 15.1 (1992), pp. 1 to 43 (text not read). K1.label: Taught (wider rule), all branches
K1.reason: Rule 7. Deciding texts. Śvetāmbara branch (all three sub-branches): Ācārāṅga I.4.1 (Tier 1, Explicit, wider rule). It says no breathing, existing, living or sentient creature may be slain, abused or tormented, and calls this 'the pure, unchangeable, eternal law'. Supporting it: Ācārāṅga I.4.2, which rejects as 'the doctrine of the unworthy' any teaching that some killing carries no wrong; Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10, 'the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything'; Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2, which counts killing for one's own sake, and killing because someone has hurt, hurts or will hurt one, as sinful activity; and Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7, where the lay vow covers all movable beings, every human included. Every branch, Digambaras included: the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra (Tier 1), at Clear teaching as a wider rule. 7.1 makes abstaining from injury the first vow. 7.2 binds householders to it in a lesser form. 7.8 = 7.13 defines injury as taking life through non-vigilance or passion (the Digambara number is now seen in a search result). 7.4 (= 7.9) teaches that injury brings calamity here and evil hereafter. These texts reach every person from birth onwards. Rules 2 and 3 are not met. No counted text found lets a private person kill someone who is not attacking. None permits killing newborns or children. None lets a master, husband or parent kill those in his power (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 condemns even harsh punishment of them). None makes a killing blameless because of the victim's faith, status or deeds (Ācārāṅga I.4.2 rejects any such doctrine; Tattvārtha 7.6 = 7.11 asks for equanimity, not hostility, towards the ill-behaved). None limits protection to Jains. The nearest counted counter-text, new in this pass, is Gautama's analogy in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7: a man does not break his word by putting to death a 'renegade' householder. It is a hypothetical about how far a vow reaches. 'Does not break his vow' is not 'blameless': the same reply says killing immovable beings does not break the lay vow, and the canon still counts that as injury bringing bad karma. Nothing in it approves the killing, so it is Implied and does not decide (rule 4). The lay vow's one exception, 'except on the order of an established authority' (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7, now seen in a search summary), is a ruler's order: context (rule 5). Consistency with the cross-tradition hard cases: Jainism has no counted text like a kinsman's or a zealot's licensed killing (Numbers 35:26 to 27, 'no bloodguilt'; Phinehas, Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31), a master killing a slave woman with no retaliation due (Abū Dāwūd 4361), drowning weak newborns (De Ira 1.15.2), killing a class of people without retribution (the icchantika), resisting or wronging the follower of the Lie (Yasna 31.18, 33.2) or rites against enemies (Atharvaveda; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12). Unlike Numbers 35:27, the II.7 analogy declares no absence of guilt, only that a particular vow was kept, so it is not treated as the same kind of text. The nearest Tier 2 items are not counted. The Niśītha Cūrṇi (Mūrtipūjaka only) is known only from secondary reports, which as described concern defence of the order or of a nun under assault (K1's exception). The Viṣṇukumāra story is unverified narrative about a royal persecutor. Caveats: (1) no deciding row has been read directly. All are VERIFIED (search), and the Tattvārtha rows only through secondary sites, so under METHOD decision 6 the label is provisional. (2) The Digambara case rests on the shared sūtra, which does not itself say which part of the vow householders keep (the Tier 2 Ratnakaraṇḍaka 3.53 puts intentional injury of any moving being inside it). (3) The 'harmless (innocent) beings' limit of the Śvetāmbara lay vow is seen only in modern exposition, and Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra 2.19 (Tier 2) is unverified. If a classical commentary let a lay person kill a non-attacking 'offender' on his own authority, the Śvetāmbara lay case would become a rule 6 hard case. Even then Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 would stand. (4) The full text of the II.7 analogy, including who made the vow and on what terms, was not seen. A reviewer should read sacred-texts.com sbe4571.

K0.label: Taught, all branches (Explicit for Śvetāmbaras; Clear teaching for Digambaras through the shared text)
K0.reason: Rule 7. K0 is narrower than K1, so every text that teaches K1 teaches K0. Śvetāmbaras: Explicit on K0's own terms. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 (Tier 1) names injury done for one's own sake as the first kind of sinful activity. It names as the third ('slaying') killing because one thinks someone has hurt, hurts or will hurt oneself or one's own, which covers both revenge and pre-emptive killing; both bring bad karma to the doer. Ācārāṅga I.4.1 is Explicit as a wider rule. Every branch: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.8 = 7.13 defines the injury that 7.1 forbids by pramatta-yoga. The Śvetāmbara-numbered edition's commentary reads this as negligence and wrong motive, and a study book as negligence, attachment or aversion. Digambara-numbered renderings give 'the severance of vitalities out of passion' (Sangave, citing 7/13; the rendering Wikipedia attributes to Vijay K. Jain's edition with the Sarvārthasiddhi). Killing out of greed, anger or hatred is therefore a central case, at Clear teaching close to Explicit (the passion gloss is translation and commentary, not the sūtra's bare words). Tattvārtha 7.4 (= 7.9) adds that injury brings calamity here and evil hereafter. No counted text permits such a killing. The Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 'renegade' analogy says nothing about motive and does not approve the killing (rule 4). Caveat: all rows are search-verified only, and the Tattvārtha rows only through secondary sites.

K3.label: Taught (wider rule), all branches; no counted text names non-combatants
K3.reason: Rule 7, applied to K3. Two sets of texts forbid killing any being and so reach non-combatants: the Śvetāmbara wider rule (Ācārāṅga I.4.1, Explicit, no exception) and, for every branch, the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.1 with 7.8 = 7.13 and 7.4 (Clear teaching). Killing someone who is not fighting cannot count as defensive injury under the lay allowance. Rules 2 and 3 are not met: no counted text permits killing non-combatants. The war texts are Implied only. Bhagavatī 7.9 (verified by search) approves a lay soldier, compelled by the king, the assembly and the army, who strikes only the man who strikes him first. It also corrects the belief that those killed in battle go to heaven: most are reborn in hell or as animals. Uttarādhyayana 9.34 to 35 ranks self-conquest above conquest. The label depends on one reading. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 (Śvetāmbara, partly verified by search) gives the lay vow against injuring movable beings with the exception 'except on the order of an established authority'. Read as saying what the vow does not cover, without saying the excepted act is right, it presupposes rather than approves (rule 4). That is the reading applied to the same text for K1. If the project rules instead that a vow exception counts as permission, K3 becomes Unclear for the Śvetāmbara branch (rule 6), because no text checked settles whether the exception would release a lay soldier ordered to kill non-combatants. That ruling should then apply to every tradition's texts on duress and royal orders. Somadeva's Tier 2 statement that kings use weapons only against armed enemies is unverified.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The K1 reason says the lay vow's one exception in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7, 'except on the order of an established authority', 'is a ruler's order: context (rule 5)'. That has not been shown. The row itself leaves open whether the exception covers orders from people who are not rulers. On its face, 'established authority' could mean a community, a guild, a family head or a strong man. A killing on such an order is not imposed through a court or a ruler, so exclusion (a) would not cover it. The strongest case against the label runs like this. Suppose the exception is read as permission and it reaches private authorities. Then a counted Śvetāmbara text permits a deliberate killing that K1 forbids. That is rule 3 (Contradicted in one branch), or rule 6 (Unclear) while its reach is unsettled. The case fails only under rule 4. An exception says what a vow does not cover, and the same canon still counts all injury not renounced as sinful activity that brings bad karma (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2; Ācārāṅga I.4.1). The K3 reason already applies this rule 4 reading to the same clause, but the K1 reason leans on rule 5 instead. So the two reasons are inconsistent.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 4, 5 and 6. Rule 2's 'graded protection' (an act that stays a fault is not thereby permitted). Consistency between the K1 and K3 reasons on the same text.
objections.proposed: Base K1's treatment of the exception on rule 4 first, and say that whether it is judicial or private (rule 5) is unresolved. Add to K1 the conditional that is already in K3: if the project counts a vow exception as permission, Śvetāmbara K1 becomes Unclear (rule 6) until the reach of 'established authority' is settled, and that ruling must then apply to every tradition's texts on vows, duress and orders. Lead for a reviewer (from memory, unverified, not used as evidence): in Upāsakadaśā 1, Ānanda's vow about other teachers is said to carry six exceptions (compulsion by the king, the community, a strong man or a god, by elders, or for livelihood). If so, 'abhioga' in Śvetāmbara lay formulas may be wider than a ruler's order. Check Jacobi's note on II.7 and the Prakrit.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Caveat (2) says the shared sūtra does not say which part of the vow householders keep, and fills the gap with the Tier 2 Ratnakaraṇḍaka 3.53. But a counted shared row already in the table narrows that gap, and the K1 reason does not cite it. Tattvārtha 7.20 = 7.25 lists binding, beating, mutilating, overloading and withholding food and drink as lapses of the householder's vow of non-injury. So the shared text itself places beings in one's power (dependants, servants, animals) inside the householder's vow, even against lesser harms, and killing them is covered all the more. For a stranger who is not in one's power, the Digambara case still rests on 7.4 = 7.9 and 7.8 = 7.13 (injury as such is evil), not on the vow, and the reason should say so. Separately, 'Rules 2 and 3 are not met' is stated without saying what was searched. The Digambara-only counted texts (Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, Kaṣāyapāhuḍa, Kundakunda's works, Mūlācāra) were not searched for counter-evidence; only Pravacanasāra 3.17 was searched, and it was not found. The Śvetāmbara Chedasūtras (Niśītha, Bṛhatkalpa, Vyavahāra) are Tier 1 in both canons and were not checked either, even though the reported emergency rules sit in their commentaries.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 1, 3 and 7. The branch rule in corpus.md. METHOD section 3: look for evidence against, not only for.
objections.proposed: Cite 7.20 = 7.25 in K1 as shared Tier 1 evidence of what the householder keeps. Say that 'rules 2 and 3 are not met' holds for the texts checked, and list the Digambara-only Tier 1 texts and the Śvetāmbara Chedasūtras as not checked.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The shared case, and so the whole Digambara case, rests on Tattvārtha 7.8 = 7.13, which defines injury by the doer's state of mind (non-vigilance or passion). This is the one route by which someone could argue that a deliberate killing of a non-attacker is not injury: the killing is claimed to be done without passion, for a good end. The route is in use. The secondary report on the Niśītha Cūrṇi gives a modern book's reading that force used without selfish motive or hatred counts as non-violent. And the surgeon example in the Śvetāmbara-numbered commentary shows that the definition does leave some deliberate harms out. If a classical commentary applied that reading to a killing outside defence, it would narrow the shared text (rule 6). The K1 reason names neither this risk nor the tradition's own answer to it.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (a reading narrowed by classical commentators). METHOD section 3, rule 3: show the tradition's own reconciliation.
objections.proposed: Name the risk and the reconciliation in the K1 reason. Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 79 to 89 (Digambara, Tier 2, verified in outline) rejects religion, mercy and the victim's state as excuses for killing. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 counts pre-emptive killing as sinful whatever reason is claimed. The surgeon example concerns a needed act done for the good of the person harmed. The Niśītha Cūrṇi cases, as reported, are defence cases. No label change unless a verified classical commentary applies the 'no passion' reading to killing a non-attacker.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Two points on the Niśītha Cūrṇi. (i) The row says the tradition places the cūrṇis below the Āgamas, but cites no source for this. Mūrtipūjakas are commonly described as holding the 'five-limbed' canon (pañcāṅgī: the sūtra with its niryukti, bhāṣya, cūrṇi and ṭīkā) as authoritative. That description is from general knowledge, to be checked. Whether this places the cūrṇis alongside primary scripture under METHOD decision 4 has not been decided. If it does, the Niśītha Cūrṇi becomes a counted text for the Mūrtipūjaka branch. The reported dictum that 'an enemy of Dharma must be punished' would then be the main risk of a zealot-type case: rule 3 for that branch, or rule 6 if its defensive character is disputed, as with the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra in Buddhism. (ii) The K1 reason says the reports 'concern defence of the order or of a nun under assault (K1's exception)'. A nun under assault is inside the exception. 'Defence of the order' is inside it only where persons face killing or grave harm, not where the threat is to an institution, its property or its standing.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 and METHOD section 9, decision 4. Rules 3, 5 and 6. The wording of K1's exception.
objections.proposed: Record the tier question as open: decision 4 has not yet been applied to the pañcāṅgī. Say that the label holds because the passages are unverified at the primary level, not because of their tier alone. Narrow the words '(K1's exception)' to the nun case and to defence of persons. A reviewer should read Granoff (1992), whose existence the rows confirm, for any primary passage approving force against a persecutor who was not attacking at the time.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The Viṣṇukumāra row says the persecutor 'holds royal office in the story, so it is at most context (rule 5)'. Rule 5 covers killings imposed through a court or a ruler. Here the killer is a monk acting on his own authority, and the victim's office does not make the act judicial. If a version in a counted text approved the killing, the question would be K1's exception (was the minister then threatening to kill or gravely harm the monks?), not rule 5. The Buddhist record uses rules 5 and 6 for the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra because there the killer is a king. That is the opposite case.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 5. K1's exception. Consistency with the Buddhist treatment of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
objections.proposed: Reword the row's bearing. No label change, because the story is unverified and not a counted text.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Caveat (3) says that if a classical commentary let a lay person kill a non-attacking 'offender', the Śvetāmbara lay case 'would become a rule 6 hard case'. That overstates the risk. An 'innocent' (nirāgas) qualifier in a lay vow says only which killings break the vow, and the canon still counts the rest as injury. Under rule 2 that is graded protection, not permission. It would not narrow the deciding text, Ācārāṅga I.4.1, which says nothing about lay vows. Rule 6 would apply only if a classical commentator said such a killing is right or free of fault.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 (graded protection is not permission). Rule 6.
objections.proposed: Restate caveat (3) to say this: if Yogaśāstra 2.19 is verified with 'innocent', record graded protection in the lay vow, and make the label Unclear only if the commentary approves or clears the killing.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The strongest case for rules 2 and 3 is the 'renegade' analogy in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7. In this counted Śvetāmbara text, Gautama, the founder's chief disciple and a teacher within the text, answers that a man who puts a 'renegade' householder to death does not break his word. Read one way, a teacher affirms that killing a person carries no breach because of what the victim did. The case fails on four counts. 'Does not break his word' is about a vow's scope, not a statement that the act is right or free of fault. The same reply applies the point to killing immovable beings, which the canon counts as sinful (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2). The vow-takers in the analogy are hypothetical. And unlike Numbers 35:27 ('no bloodguilt') or Abū Dāwūd 4361 (no retaliation due), it declares no absence of guilt or penalty. Implied is right. However, only an outline of the passage was seen. One sentence approving the killing would move it to rule 3.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 2, 3 and 4. Consistency with Numbers 35:26 to 27 and Abū Dāwūd 4361.
objections.proposed: Keep it Implied, and make it a priority for direct reading (sacred-texts.com sbe4571) before admission.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The deciding Śvetāmbara row, Ācārāṅga I.4.1, was verified from search summaries that never quoted its prohibiting clause. Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10 ('the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything') is also Explicit and a wider rule, and a search result quoted it word for word. The label should not rest only on the less well verified of the two. The label text also leaves out 'provisional', although every deciding row is VERIFIED (search) only, and the Tattvārtha rows only through secondary sites.
objections.proposed: Name Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10 together as the deciding Śvetāmbara texts, and add 'provisional' to the label itself.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: For Digambaras the label rates the passion-based teaching 'Clear teaching close to Explicit'. But the passion reading of 'pramatta' comes from translations and Tier 2 commentary; the bare word means heedless or non-vigilant. So the strength rating leans on Tier 2. K0 does not need that support. Tattvārtha 7.1 with 7.2 and 7.4 = 7.9 teaches K0 as a wider rule at Clear teaching whatever the gloss, because a deliberate killing for gain or revenge is non-vigilant on any reading. For Śvetāmbaras, Explicit holds: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 names injury for one's own sake (kind 1) and revenge or pre-emptive killing (kind 3) as sinful activity that brings bad karma.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 (Tier 2 may clarify but not raise strength). Rule 7.
objections.proposed: Digambara level: Clear teaching (wider rule), dropping 'close to Explicit'. The label is unchanged.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The K3 reason says killing non-combatants 'cannot count as defensive injury under the lay allowance'. That allowance is the fourfold division of injury, which is modern exposition with no traced classical source, so it cannot carry any part of the label (rule 1). It also cuts both ways: some summaries extend defensive injury to 'enemies in battle' and 'defending one's country' without saying who counts as an enemy. Meanwhile the K3 reason leaves out the strongest counted Śvetāmbara text on the usual reason given in war. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2's third kind counts as sinful the killing of anyone one thinks 'will hurt me or mine'. That is the standard ground for killing an enemy's non-combatants, for example sons who might fight later.
objections.proposed: Drop the 'lay allowance' sentence. For Śvetāmbaras, base K3 on Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10 (no war exception) and on the third kind in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 (pre-emptive killing is sin). For every branch, base it on Tattvārtha 7.1, 7.4 = 7.9 and 7.8 = 7.13.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The Bhagavatī 7.9 row says the text 'approves, through his rebirth' a lay soldier who kills only an attacker. In what was seen, Varuṇa leaves the field, takes the monastic vows and dies before his heavenly rebirth. The rebirth may reward the renunciation, not the killing, so 'approves' overstates it (rule 4). In the other direction, the passage corrects the belief that the battle-dead go to heaven: most are reborn in hell or as animals. That is the same kind of text as SN 42.3, which the Buddhist record counts as Clear teaching for K3, applying all the more to non-combatants. The Jain row rates it Implied.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 4. Cross-tradition consistency with SN 42.3 in Buddhism.
objections.proposed: Reword: the text reports with approval a lay follower who limited himself to the man who struck first, and his rebirth follows his renunciation. After direct reading, rate the correction by the reason the passage gives. If it names killing or the will to kill as the cause of those rebirths, rate it Clear teaching (supporting) for K3; if it gives no reason, Implied.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The strongest case for Unclear on K3: the tradition's own model lay follower kills in battle. That suggests Ācārāṅga I.4.1 is not applied as a binding rule to lay soldiers, so a counted text narrows its reach in war (rule 6). The case fails because Varuṇa kills only a man who is fighting him. K3 forbids killing people who are not fighting, so any narrowing reaches combatants only, which K3 leaves open. His vow to strike only the one who strikes first follows K3's own line.
objections.proposed: Keep 'Taught' and say this explicitly in the K3 reason.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: For Digambaras, K3 rests only on the shared sūtra. Its householder vow is partial and says nothing about war, and no Digambara counted text on war was checked (Somadeva is Tier 2 and unverified). This case is weaker than the Śvetāmbara one. Across traditions, a wider rule with no war exception yields 'Taught' for K3 both in Buddhism and here. Yet Hinduism's K3 is Silent, although its K1 rests on wider rules (Chāndogya 8.15.1, Gita 16.2). Either the Hindu record shows a counted text that removes war from its wider rule (such as the Gita's call to fight), or the two treatments are inconsistent.
objections.proposed: Keep 'Taught (wider rule), all branches', and say that the Digambara case rests on the shared text alone. Flag the Hindu comparison for the cross-tradition consistency pass.

They forbid killing any living being, so they reach every person from birth (rule 9), whatever the person's faith, status or deeds. Ācārāṅga I.4.2 rejects any doctrine that some killing is free of wrong. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 counts killing for one's own sake, and killing in revenge or to forestall a feared harm, as sinful, and condemns even harsh punishment of slaves, servants, wives and children. Every branch, Digambaras included: the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra (Tier 1, Clear teaching, wider rule). 7.1 and 7.2 make abstaining from injury the first vow, binding on householders in a lesser form. 7.20 = 7.25 shows that the householder's vow covers beings in one's power, even against lesser harms. 7.8 = 7.13 defines injury as taking life through non-vigilance or passion, and 7.4 = 7.9 teaches that injury brings calamity here and evil hereafter. Rules 2 and 3 are not met in the texts checked. The Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 exception ('except on the order of an established authority') and the 'renegade' analogy say what a vow does not cover. They do not approve any killing, and the same canon still counts such injury as sinful (rule 4). A vow-scope limit is at most graded protection (rule 2). Whether the exception reaches orders from people other than rulers is unresolved, so rule 5 is not relied on. The tradition's reconciliation of the passion-based definition: Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 79 to 89 (Tier 2) rejects religion, mercy and the victim's state as excuses. Caveats. (1) All deciding rows are VERIFIED (search) only, and the Tattvārtha rows only through secondary sites (METHOD decision 6). (2) The Digambara-only Tier 1 texts and the Śvetāmbara Chedasūtras were not searched for counter-evidence. (3) The Niśītha Cūrṇi's tier for Mūrtipūjakas (the pañcāṅgī question) is undecided. It is unverified at the primary level, and as reported it concerns defence of persons. (4) If the project rules that a vow exception counts as permission, Śvetāmbara K1 becomes Unclear (rule 6) until the reach of 'established authority' is settled. Śvetāmbaras: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 (Tier 1) names injury for one's own sake (kind 1) and killing because someone has hurt, hurts or will hurt oneself or one's own (kind 3: revenge and pre-emption) as sinful activity that brings bad karma to the doer. That is Explicit on K0's own terms, and Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10 teach it as Explicit wider rules. Every branch: Tattvārtha 7.1 with 7.2, 7.4 = 7.9 and 7.8 = 7.13 is Clear teaching as a wider rule. A deliberate killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge is non-vigilant on any reading, and is a central case on the passion reading given by the Tier 2 commentary. No counted text permits such a killing. The II.7 analogy says nothing about motive and approves nothing (rule 4). Caveat: the label is search-verified only, and the Tattvārtha rows only through secondary sites.

K3.label: Taught (wider rule), all branches; provisional; no counted text names non-combatants; the Digambara case rests on the shared text alone
K3.reason: Rule 7, applied to K3. Śvetāmbara: Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10 forbid killing any being and make no war exception. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2's third kind counts as sinful the killing of anyone one thinks will hurt oneself or one's own, which is the usual reason for killing an enemy's non-combatants. Every branch: Tattvārtha 7.1, 7.4 = 7.9 and 7.8 = 7.13 (Clear teaching), with no war exception. No counted text permits killing non-combatants, so rules 2 and 3 are not met. Bhagavatī 7.9 reports with approval a lay follower, compelled to fight, who struck only the man who struck him first, and it corrects the belief that the battle-dead go to heaven. It narrows nothing that K3 forbids, because it concerns combatants only. Rate the correction after direct reading: Clear teaching (supporting) if it names killing as the cause of those rebirths, as SN 42.3 does in Buddhism, otherwise Implied. In K3, war is the subject of the wording, so the Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 exception bears directly. It is read under rule 4, as for K1. If the project counts a vow exception as permission, Śvetāmbara K3 becomes Unclear (rule 6), because no text checked says whether the exception would release a lay soldier ordered to kill non-combatants. The modern fourfold division of injury is not counted and plays no part in the label. Somadeva's statement is Tier 2 and unverified.

challenge.consistency_notes: The Jain labels sit consistently with the cross-tradition hard cases once three reasoning points are fixed: the II.7 exception is treated under rule 4, not rule 5; the Viṣṇukumāra row's use of rule 5 is corrected; and Bhagavatī 7.9 is rated in the same way as SN 42.3. (1) Numbers 35:26 to 27 declares that a private kinsman's killing carries no bloodguilt. The Jain 'renegade' analogy in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 declares no absence of guilt or penalty, only that a vow was not broken, and the same reply treats killing immovable beings, which the canon still counts as sin, in the same way. So treating it as Implied (rule 4) is consistent, provided direct reading confirms that no sentence approves the killing. (2) Phinehas (Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31) and the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's licensed killing of slanderers: the nearest Jain items are the reported Niśītha Cūrṇi dictum ('an enemy of Dharma must be punished') and the Viṣṇukumāra story. Both are unverified at the primary level and are Tier 2 or outside the corpus, so neither decides. If the project rules that Mūrtipūjakas treat the pañcāṅgī commentaries as primary and a passage is verified, it should be handled as Buddhism's Mahāparinirvāṇa was: rule 3 for that branch, or rule 6 if its defensive or judicial character is disputed. Rule 5 cannot shelter a monk who kills an official, because rule 5 covers killings imposed by rulers, not killings of them. (3) Abū Dāwūd 4361 (a master kills a slave woman and no retaliation is due): the Jain counted texts point the other way, since Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 condemns even harsh punishment of slaves and dependants, and Tattvārtha 7.20 = 7.25 counts binding and beating as lapses. (4) De Ira 1.15.2 (drowning newborns): no Jain analogue; the wider rule reaches newborns (rule 9). (5) Yasna 31.18 and 33.2: Tattvārtha 7.6 = 7.11 prescribes equanimity, not hostility, towards the ill-behaved. (6) Atharvaveda rites and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12: no counted Jain text approving harmful rites was found. Coverage was partial, though: the Chedasūtras and the Digambara-only Tier 1 texts were not searched. (7) Vow and precept scope: a Jain vow exception that leaves the act sinful is treated like rule 2's 'sin before God', which is graded protection and not permission. If the project instead counts a vow exception as permission, that ruling must apply to every tradition's texts on vows, duress and royal orders, and Śvetāmbara K1 and K3 would become Unclear. (8) K3 across traditions: Jainism and Buddhism both get 'Taught' through wider rules with no war exception, and Bhagavatī 7.9's correction of the battle-heaven belief parallels SN 42.3. Hinduism's K3 is Silent although its K1 rests on wider rules. That divergence is justified only if a counted Hindu text removes war from its wider rule, and it should be checked in the consistency pass. Leads (from memory, unverified, not used as evidence): Tattvārtha 8.1, if it lists non-abstinence (avirati) among the causes of bondage, would confirm from the shared text that injury not renounced is still binding; and the six exceptions attached to Ānanda's vow in Upāsakadaśā 1 bear on what 'abhioga' covers in II.7.
